scenes.say: Find two numbers that add up to a target. It looks like two nested loops. It needs one lookup. By the end, you'll do it in one pass, then count subarrays that sum to k.

lines.text: Two numbers that add to a target
Subarrays summing to k: one pass

scenes.say: Today's plan. Hash maps first: two sum, counting, and why lookups are fast. Then prefix sums for range sums. Finally, both together to count subarrays, plus difference arrays.
lines: Solve two sum in one pass

scenes.title: Two Sum
scenes.statement: Given an array and a target, return the indexes of two numbers that add to the target.
scenes.say: Given an array and a target, find two numbers that add to the target. For example, two, seven, eleven, fifteen, target nine. The answer: indexes zero and one. Ten thousand numbers means fifty million pairs, so we need better.

scenes.head: A coat check
scenes.say: Think of a coat check. You hand over a coat and get a ticket. Later, you show the ticket and they fetch the coat at once, never searching the rack. A hash map works the same: ticket is key, coat is value.

scenes.head: Two sum: [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9
scenes.say: Array two, seven, eleven, fifteen. Target nine. For each number, ask which partner I need. First, two. I need seven. Is seven in the map? No. Store two at index zero. Next, seven. I need two. Two is in the map! The answer is indexes zero and one.

scenes.head: Two sum in code
scenes.say: In code: a map from value to index. For each number, look up the target minus it. Found? Print both indexes. Not found? Store this number and move on. On our array it prints zero and one. One pass, O of n.
Your turn. Array three, two, four. Target six. Which indexes come back? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The classic bug: store first
scenes.say: One and two: two plus four. Now the classic bug. Store first, then look up, and three finds itself. Zero, zero. The fix: look up first, then store.

panels.label: bug
fix

scenes.title: Most frequent value
scenes.statement: Given an array, return the value that appears most often.
scenes.say: Next problem. Which value appears most often in an array? For example, three, one, three, two, three, one. The answer: three, three times. The same map solves Group Anagrams and Top K Frequent Elements.
scenes.note: same map: Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements

scenes.head: Which value appears most?
scenes.say: Which value appears most? Keep a map from value to count. First, three. A new key. Then one. Another new key. Three again: it now has two. Then two. A third key. Three, a third time: it has three. One again: it has two. The biggest count wins: three.

scenes.head: Counting in code
scenes.say: In code, the counting is one line. The line cnt of x plus plus makes a zero if the key is missing, then adds one. Then scan the map for the biggest count. It prints three, seen three times.
Your turn. A map holds three keys. Now you read the count of seven, which isn't there. How many keys does it hold after that? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `cnt` has 3 keys. After `cout << cnt[7];` its size is?

scenes.head: Reading a key creates it
scenes.say: Four. Reading cnt of seven quietly creates the key, with a zero. To check without creating, use count or find. Here count of nine says zero, and the size stays three. Then cnt of seven prints zero, and the size jumps to four.

chapters.title: Why a lookup costs one step

scenes.title: Why is a lookup O(1)?
scenes.statement: A hash map finds a key in one step on average. How does it do that, and when does it break?
scenes.say: How can a hash map find any key in one step? When does it break? For example, the key cat. The answer: hash it to a bucket, and jump straight there.

scenes.head: Key to bucket
scenes.say: Picture four buckets. Say the key is cat. A hash function is a recipe that turns any key into a number. Here it says two. So cat goes in bucket two. To find cat later, run the same recipe and jump straight there. That's the ticket from the coat check: no searching, one step on average.

changes.cue: A hash function is a recipe

scenes.say: Your turn. Now every key lands in bucket two. Cat, dog, emu, all n of them. What does one lookup cost? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: All n keys hash to the same bucket. One lookup costs?

scenes.head: When every key collides
scenes.say: O of n. Dog and emu land in bucket two too, chained one after another. To find emu, walk past cat, then dog, then reach emu. That's n steps when n keys collide. Normal hashing spreads keys out, so chains stay short.

scenes.head: map vs unordered_map
scenes.say: Last question: map or unordered map? Lookup? Sorted tree, O of log n, versus hash, O of one on average. Worst case? Map stays log n. Hashing can hit O of n. Order? Only map keeps keys sorted. Contest tip? Setters can build colliding inputs, so add a custom hash.

scenes.title: Range sum queries
scenes.statement: Answer many questions of the form: what is the sum from index l to index r?
scenes.say: New problem. Answer many questions: what is the sum from index l to r? For example, one, two, three, minus two, two, from index one to three. The answer: three. We want each answer instantly.
scenes.note: many queries: no re-adding each time

scenes.head: A car odometer
scenes.say: Think of a car odometer. At the start of a trip it reads thirty. At the end, eighty. The trip was fifty kilometers: one subtraction. A prefix sum array is an odometer for your array.

scenes.head: Running totals of [1, 2, 3, -2, 2]
scenes.say: Array one, two, three, minus two, two. Build a running total, called p. Start at zero. Add one: one. Add two: three. Add three: six. Add minus two: four. Add two: six. Now the sum from index one to three? Take p at four, which is four. Subtract p at one, which is one. Four minus one is three.

scenes.head: Prefix sums in code
scenes.say: In code, p has n plus one slots, all zero. Each slot is the one before it, plus the next number. Build is O of n. Print p, and the query: p at four, minus p at one. Zero, one, three, six, four, six, then three.
Your turn. Same array. What is the sum of index zero to three? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Why p has n + 1 slots
scenes.say: Four. P at four is four, minus p at zero, which is zero. Check: one plus two plus three minus two is four. Why p zero? A range starting at index zero needs an empty prefix to subtract. That's the plus one in n plus one slots.

scenes.head: Three traps
scenes.say: Three traps. P of r minus p of l misses a of r. Use r plus one. Sums past two billion overflow an int. Use long long. Updates between queries? Prefix sums are static. Use a Fenwick tree.

scenes.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
scenes.statement: Count the subarrays whose elements add up to exactly k.
scenes.say: The famous problem. Count the subarrays whose sum is exactly k. For example, the same array, with k equal to three. The answer: four subarrays. Two nested loops would work, but we want one pass.
scenes.note: brute force O(n²); target: one pass

scenes.head: Turn it into a lookup
scenes.say: Now the famous one: count subarrays with sum k. A subarray's sum is the prefix at its end, minus the prefix just before it. That should equal k, so the earlier prefix must equal the current prefix minus k. Finding a value is exactly what a map does.

scenes.head: k = 3, walk the totals (1/2)
scenes.say: Walk the totals, with k equal to three. The map starts with zero seen once, the empty prefix. Total one. Need minus two. None. Store one. Total three. Need zero. One match. Store three. Total six. Need three. Match again. Store six.

scenes.head: k = 3, walk the totals (2/2)
scenes.say: Two more totals. Total four. Need one. A match. Store four. Total six again. Need three. Another match. Store six. Four subarrays in all.

scenes.head: Subarray sum equals k
scenes.say: In code, the map starts with zero seen once. Keep a running sum. For each number, add it, then add how often sum minus k was seen. Then record the sum. It prints four. One pass, O of n.
Your turn. Delete the zero seed from the map. The array is just three, and k is three. What comes back? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Trap: forget the seed
scenes.say: Zero, and that's wrong. The answer is one: the subarray three itself. It starts at index zero, so no prefix sits before it. The seed stands for that empty prefix. Without it, you lose every subarray that starts at the beginning.

panels.label: no seed

scenes.title: Many range updates
scenes.statement: Apply many updates of the form add v to indexes l to r, then print the final array.
scenes.say: Last problem. Many updates, each adding a value to a range. For example, add five to indexes one to three, in six zeros. The answer: zero, five, five, five, zero, zero.

scenes.head: Mark the start and the stop
scenes.say: Now the mirror image: many range updates. Think of a heater schedule: on at day one, off at day four. Mark just those two days, then sweep the days with a running total.

scenes.head: Add 5 to indexes 1 to 3
scenes.say: Task: add five to indexes one to three, without touching each one. Plus five at index one. Minus five at index four, where the range stops. Now sweep a running total. Zero, five, five, five, zero, zero. Two steps per update, however long the range.

scenes.head: Difference array in code
scenes.say: In code: zeros, then the range from l to r with value v. Add v at l. Subtract v at r plus one. Then one pass of running total. It prints zero, five, five, five, zero, zero.
Your turn. Also add two to indexes two to four. What does the final array look like? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Also add 2 to indexes 2 to 4. Final array?

scenes.head: Two updates, one sweep
scenes.say: Zero, five, seven, seven, two, zero. The second update marks plus two at index two, and minus two at index five. Sweep again, and the two stacks on top of the five.

scenes.head: Difference array traps
scenes.say: Two traps. Subtracting at r, not r plus one, stops the range a cell early. And r plus one can equal n, so the array needs n plus one slots. Many big updates can also overflow, so use long long.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Two sum? Look up target minus x, store x. One pass. Counting? Map value to count. Why O of one? Hash the key, jump to its bucket.
rows: Two sum with a hash map?
look up target − x, then store x: O(n)
hash the key, jump to its bucket (average)

scenes.head: The follow-ups
scenes.say: Worst case? O of n if everything collides, so contest code uses a custom hash. Map versus unordered map? Map is a sorted tree, log n. Unordered is a hash. Common mistake? Inserting first, so a number pairs with itself.
rows: O(n) if all collide: use a custom hash
sorted tree O(log n) vs hash O(1)
insert first: x pairs with itself

scenes.say: Quick self test. You read the count of a key that is not in the map. What comes back, and what happens to the size? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `cnt[x]` for a missing key: result and size?

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Prefix sums? A running total, built once in O of n. Any range sum is one subtraction. Subarray sum equals k? Count earlier prefixes equal to sum minus k.

scenes.head: The follow-ups
scenes.say: Difference array? Mark plus v at the start, minus v after the end, then sweep. Why n plus one entries? Zero is the empty prefix. Updates between queries? Prefix sums are static, so use a Fenwick tree.
rows: two marks per update, one sweep

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode one, Two Sum, is today's first lookup. LeetCode five sixty, Subarray Sum Equals K, is prefix sums plus a map. LeetCode eleven oh nine, Corporate Flight Bookings, is a difference array.
rows: look up the partner, then store
prefix sums + a map of counts

scenes.say: So say this. A hash map turns a search into one lookup. A running total turns any range sum into a subtraction. Together, they count subarrays in one pass.
lines: A hash map: one lookup instead of a search.
Prefix sums: any range sum is one subtraction.
Together: count subarrays in one pass, O(n).
